outputs.L3:
The text investigates variations of two-dimensional surfaces swept out by closed strings as they evolve through a spacetime manifold. These worldsheets are treated as geometric objects whose dynamics are determined by the Nambu–Goto action, which measures the area of the surface. Varying this action yields the geodesic surface equation, the string-theoretic analogue of the geodesic equation for a point particle.

The analysis then considers infinitesimal variations between neighboring geodesic surfaces. From these variations, the geodesic surface deviation equation is derived. This equation generalizes the familiar geodesic deviation equation and describes how nearby string worldsheets separate or converge under the influence of spacetime curvature. Its solutions define Jacobi fields along the geodesic surface, encoding infinitesimal deformations through a family of extremal worldsheets.

An index form is subsequently introduced for the geodesic surface, in direct analogy with the index form used in point-particle geometry. This bilinear form captures the second variation of the Nambu–Goto action and provides information about the stability and local extremality of the worldsheet. Finally, the index form is used to characterize conjugate strings: closed-string configurations connected by a nontrivial Jacobi field that vanishes, or satisfies the appropriate boundary conditions, at both configurations. The existence of such conjugate strings signals a loss of local minimality or stability of the geodesic surface.
outputs.L4:
A relativistic closed string traces out a two-dimensional surface, or worldsheet, as it evolves through spacetime. The geometry of this surface is described by an embedding \(X^\mu(\tau,\sigma)\), where \(\tau\) is an evolution parameter and the spatial parameter \(\sigma\) is periodic. The tangent vectors \(e_a^{\mu}=\partial_aX^\mu\) induce the worldsheet metric

\[
h_{ab}=g_{\mu\nu}e_a^\mu e_b^\nu ,
\]

with \(g_{\mu\nu}\) denoting the spacetime metric. The dynamics follow from the Nambu–Goto action,

\[
S[X]=-T\int d^2\xi\,\sqrt{-\det h},
\]

which measures the invariant area of the worldsheet and generalizes the proper-time action of a point particle.

Varying the embedding while keeping the relevant boundary data fixed gives the geodesic surface equation,

\[
D_a\!\left(\sqrt{-h}\,h^{ab}\partial_bX^\mu\right)=0,
\]

or, equivalently, the condition that the mean-curvature vector of the worldsheet vanish. Thus a classical string sweeps out an extremal surface in spacetime, just as a freely falling point particle follows an extremal curve. In a curved background, this equation includes both the intrinsic geometry of the worldsheet and the spacetime connection.

To investigate nearby string trajectories, consider a one-parameter family of extremal worldsheets \(X^\mu(\tau,\sigma;\varepsilon)\). The variation field

\[
\eta^\mu=\left.\frac{\partial X^\mu}{\partial\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
\]

measures the infinitesimal separation between neighboring worldsheets. Linearizing the geodesic surface equation produces the surface-deviation, or Jacobi, equation. Its physically relevant components are normal to the worldsheet; tangential components largely correspond to reparametrizations. In a normal frame \(n_i^\mu\), with \(\eta^\mu=\eta^i n_i^\mu\), the equation has the schematic form

\[
D_aD^a\eta^i+
\left(
K^{i}_{ab}K^{ab}{}_{j}
+
R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}
n^{\mu i}e_a^\nu e^{a\rho}n^\sigma{}_j
\right)\eta^j=0,
\]

up to sign conventions. Here \(K^i_{ab}\) is the second fundamental form of the worldsheet, and the curvature term describes tidal effects produced by the surrounding spacetime. Solutions of this equation are Jacobi fields and characterize infinitesimal deformations through neighboring extremal string worldsheets.

The second variation of the Nambu–Goto action defines an index form analogous to the index form used in geodesic theory for point particles. For normal variation fields \(\eta\) and \(\zeta\), it can be written schematically as

\[
I(\eta,\zeta)
=
\int_{\Sigma}\sqrt{-h}\,
\left[
(D_a\eta^i)(D^a\zeta_i)
-
\eta^i\mathcal{V}_{ij}\zeta^j
\right]d^2\xi ,
\]

where \(\mathcal{V}_{ij}\) contains the spacetime-curvature and extrinsic-curvature contributions. Boundary terms vanish when the variations satisfy the imposed endpoint conditions, while periodicity in \(\sigma\) ensures that the deformed objects remain closed strings. The associated Euler–Lagrange equation is precisely the Jacobi equation.

This index form determines whether an extremal worldsheet is stable under admissible deformations. Positive or negative directions of the quadratic form describe how the worldsheet area changes to second order, while zero modes correspond to nontrivial Jacobi fields. In this way, the index form connects local variation theory with the global geometry of the family of string worldsheets.

The point-particle notion of conjugate points is thereby extended to conjugate strings. Two closed-string configurations lying on the same extremal worldsheet are conjugate if there exists a nonzero Jacobi field that satisfies the required periodicity and vanishes on both string configurations. Such a field represents an infinitesimal family of neighboring geodesic surfaces that intersect the original surface along those strings. The appearance of a conjugate string signals a loss of local extremality or a degeneracy of the second variation.

The resulting framework provides a systematic means of studying the focusing, stability, and multiplicity of classical string worldsheets in curved spacetime. By combining the Nambu–Goto equations, the surface-deviation equation, Jacobi fields, and the index form, it generalizes familiar results from geodesic geometry to extended one-dimensional objects and supplies the geometric tools needed to identify and analyze conjugate strings on extremal surfaces.
outputs.L5:
## Using the Nambu–Goto Action in String Theory

The Nambu–Goto action is one of the simplest ways to describe the motion of a relativistic string. Named after physicists Yoichiro Nambu and Tetsuo Goto, it extends the concept of a point particle’s worldline to the two-dimensional surface, or *worldsheet*, traced by a string as it moves through spacetime.

Using the Nambu–Goto action, the dynamics of a string are determined by minimizing the area of its worldsheet. The action is written as

\[
S_{\text{NG}}=-T\int d^2\sigma \,
\sqrt{-\det(\gamma_{ab})},
\]

where \(T\) is the string tension, \(\sigma^a\) are the worldsheet coordinates, and \(\gamma_{ab}\) is the induced metric:

\[
\gamma_{ab}
=
\partial_a X^\mu \partial_b X^\nu g_{\mu\nu}.
\]

Here, \(X^\mu(\sigma)\) describes how the string worldsheet is embedded in spacetime, while \(g_{\mu\nu}\) represents the spacetime metric.

The main advantage of using the Nambu–Goto formulation is its clear geometric meaning. Just as a free relativistic particle follows a path of extremal proper length, a free string sweeps out a worldsheet of extremal area. However, the square root and determinant make direct calculations difficult. For this reason, physicists often replace the Nambu–Goto action with the classically equivalent Polyakov action, which introduces an independent worldsheet metric and is easier to quantize.

Despite these technical challenges, the Nambu–Goto action remains fundamental to string theory. It provides an intuitive description of relativistic strings and serves as a starting point for studying string motion, symmetries, equations of motion, and the geometry of extended objects.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize how variations of a closed-string worldsheet in spacetime lead from the Nambu–Goto action to geodesic surface and deviation equations.
counterfactuals.output:
Let a closed string sweep out a two-dimensional worldsheet \(\Sigma\) in a spacetime \((M,g_{\mu\nu})\), described by an embedding
\[
X^\mu(\sigma^a),\qquad a=0,1,
\]
with periodic spatial coordinate. Define tangent vectors and induced metric by
\[
e_a^{\mu}=\partial_aX^\mu,\qquad
\gamma_{ab}=g_{\mu\nu}e_a^\mu e_b^\nu .
\]

### 1. Nambu–Goto action

The string action is proportional to the worldsheet area:
\[
S_{\rm NG}[X]=-T\int_\Sigma d^2\sigma\,\sqrt{-\gamma}.
\]

Under \(X^\mu\to X^\mu+\delta X^\mu\), the variation can be integrated by parts. Because the string is closed, there is no boundary contribution. One obtains
\[
\delta S_{\rm NG}
=T\int_\Sigma \sqrt{-\gamma}\,
g_{\mu\nu}H^\mu\,\delta X^\nu ,
\]
where
\[
H^\mu=\gamma^{ab}
\left(
\partial_a\partial_bX^\mu
+\Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\partial_aX^\rho\partial_bX^\sigma
-\Gamma^c{}_{ab}\partial_cX^\mu
\right)
\]
is the mean-curvature vector of the embedded worldsheet.

Thus the Euler–Lagrange equation is
\[
H^\mu=0.
\]

This is the **geodesic-surface** or **minimal-surface equation**: the worldsheet has vanishing mean extrinsic curvature. It is the two-dimensional analogue of the point-particle geodesic equation.

In conformal gauge it becomes the wave-map equation
\[
D_a\partial^aX^\mu=0,
\]
supplemented by the Virasoro constraints
\[
g_{\mu\nu}\partial_\pm X^\mu\partial_\pm X^\nu=0.
\]

### 2. Families of worldsheets and deviation fields

Now consider a one-parameter family of classical worldsheets,
\[
X^\mu(\sigma,\varepsilon),
\]
and define the separation or deviation field
\[
\eta^\mu=\left.\frac{\partial X^\mu}{\partial\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}.
\]

Linearizing the geodesic-surface equation around a solution gives a worldsheet version of geodesic deviation. In a covariant gauge its schematic form is
\[
D_aD^a\eta^\mu
+R^\mu{}_{\nu\rho\sigma}\,
e_a^\nu\,\eta^\rho\,e^{a\sigma}
=0,
\]
together with the linearized constraints. The curvature term measures the relative focusing or defocusing of nearby worldsheets due to spacetime curvature.

Tangential components of \(\eta^\mu\) largely correspond to worldsheet reparametrizations. For the physical normal deformation
\[
\eta^\mu=\eta^i n_i^\mu,
\]
the equation is the minimal-surface Jacobi equation,
\[
(D^\perp_aD^{\perp a}\eta)^i
+
\left[
K^i{}_{ab}K_j{}^{ab}
+
R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}
n^{i\mu}e_a^\nu e^{a\rho}n_j^\sigma
\right]\eta^j=0,
\]
up to curvature-sign conventions. Here \(K^i{}_{ab}\) is the second fundamental form and \(D^\perp_a\) is the normal-bundle covariant derivative.

Hence the progression is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Nambu--Goto area}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{first variation}}\;
H^\mu=0
\;\xrightarrow{\text{linearization/second variation}}\;
\text{Jacobi or worldsheet-deviation equation}
}
\]

The first variation selects extremal worldsheets; the second variation describes how neighboring extremal worldsheets separate and determines their stability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the extension of geodesic deviation and conjugate-point theory from point particles to Nambu–Goto strings.
counterfactuals.output:
For a point particle, geodesic deviation describes how nearby geodesics separate. For a Nambu–Goto string, the analogous object is the deviation of nearby **extremal worldsheets**. The ordinary Jacobi equation becomes a covariant wave-type equation on the two-dimensional worldsheet, acting on its transverse normal deformations.

## 1. Point-particle case

A geodesic \(x^\mu(\tau)\), with tangent \(u^\mu\), obeys
\[
\nabla_u u^\mu=0.
\]
If \(\xi^\mu\) is the separation vector to a nearby geodesic, its physical transverse part satisfies the Jacobi equation
\[
\nabla_u^2\xi^\mu
+R^\mu{}_{\nu\rho\sigma}u^\nu\xi^\rho u^\sigma=0.
\]

Two points on the geodesic are conjugate if there is a nonzero Jacobi field that vanishes at both points. Equivalently, the second variation of the geodesic action has a zero mode. Conjugate points therefore signal loss of local extremality and the formation of caustics.

## 2. Nambu–Goto worldsheets

Let the string embedding be
\[
X^\mu(\sigma^a),\qquad a=0,1,
\]
with tangent vectors
\[
e_a^\mu=\partial_aX^\mu
\]
and induced metric
\[
\gamma_{ab}=g_{\mu\nu}e_a^\mu e_b^\nu.
\]
The Nambu–Goto action is
\[
S_{\rm NG}=-T\int_\Sigma d^2\sigma\,\sqrt{-\gamma}.
\]

Choose orthonormal normal vectors \(n_i^\mu\), where \(i=1,\ldots,D-2\). The second fundamental form is
\[
K_{ab}{}^i
=n^i_\mu\nabla_a e_b^\mu,
\]
up to the conventional overall sign. Varying the area gives
\[
K^i\equiv \gamma^{ab}K_{ab}{}^i=0.
\]
Thus a classical Nambu–Goto worldsheet is a timelike extremal surface, just as a particle trajectory is an extremal curve.

## 3. Physical string deviation fields

A deformation of the embedding can be decomposed as
\[
\delta X^\mu=\xi^a e_a^\mu+\Phi^i n_i^\mu.
\]

- The tangential part \(\xi^a e_a^\mu\) is, locally, a worldsheet reparametrization.
- The physical displacement is therefore the normal field
  \[
  \Phi^i(\sigma)n_i^\mu.
  \]

Because the normal frame can rotate along the worldsheet, one uses the normal-bundle derivative
\[
\mathcal D_a\Phi^i
=\partial_a\Phi^i+\omega_a{}^i{}_j\Phi^j,
\]
where \(\omega_a{}^i{}_j\) is the normal connection.

Linearizing the equation \(K^i=0\) gives the **string Jacobi equation**
\[
\mathcal D_a\mathcal D^a\Phi^i
+\mathcal M^i{}_j\Phi^j=0,
\]
with
\[
\mathcal M^i{}_j
=
K_{ab}{}^iK^{ab}{}_j
+
R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\,
n^{\mu i}e_a^\nu e^{a\rho}n^\sigma{}_j .
\]
Signs may be reversed depending on the definitions of the Riemann tensor, extrinsic curvature, and Jacobi operator.

This is the direct extension of geodesic deviation:

\[
\text{ODE along a worldline}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{hyperbolic PDE on a worldsheet}.
\]

The two contributions to the effective “tidal matrix” are:

1. **Ambient curvature:** the spacetime Riemann tensor produces tidal focusing.
2. **Extrinsic curvature:** different parts of a curved string worldsheet couple through \(K_{ab}{}^iK^{ab}{}_j\).

For codimension greater than one, the different normal polarizations also mix through the normal connection and the matrix \(\mathcal M^i{}_j\).

## 4. Second variation and stability

For an on-shell worldsheet, the quadratic variation has the schematic form
\[
\delta^2S_{\rm NG}
\propto
\int_\Sigma \sqrt{-\gamma}\,
\left[
\mathcal D_a\Phi_i\,\mathcal D^a\Phi^i
-\Phi_i\mathcal M^i{}_j\Phi^j
\right],
\]
plus boundary terms. Its Euler–Lagrange equation is the string Jacobi equation.

Hence:

- a Jacobi field is an infinitesimal deformation through nearby classical worldsheets;
- a zero mode of the second-variation operator is a degeneracy of the extremal surface;
- negative modes, in an appropriate Euclidean or boundary-value formulation, indicate instability or failure of minimality.

For a Lorentzian worldsheet, the Jacobi operator is hyperbolic rather than elliptic, so stability is naturally treated as an initial-value problem. Morse-index statements are clearest after Euclidean continuation or for suitable finite boundary-value problems.

## 5. Generalized conjugate points

A string has no single distinguished point evolving along a one-dimensional curve. Accordingly, conjugacy is generally a relation between **worldsheet boundaries or spatial string slices**.

Suppose the worldsheet lies between two spacelike slices \(C_0\) and \(C_1\). They are conjugate relative to the extremal worldsheet if there exists a nonzero normal Jacobi field satisfying
\[
\Phi^i|_{C_0}=0,
\qquad
\Phi^i|_{C_1}=0,
\]
together with the appropriate open- or closed-string boundary conditions.

Equivalently:

- the Jacobi boundary-value problem has a nontrivial kernel;
- the second variation is degenerate;
- nearby classical worldsheets with the same boundary data fail to be locally unique;
- the functional map from initial deformation data to the final string profile becomes singular.

Thus a particle conjugate point becomes, for strings, a **conjugate string configuration, conjugate slice, or focal set**. It need not be a single spacetime point; it may be a curve or a more complicated caustic structure on or near the worldsheet.

For open strings, the endpoint boundary conditions matter. Dirichlet, Neumann, or D-brane boundary conditions induce corresponding conditions on \(\Phi^i\). For closed strings, \(\Phi^i\) must be periodic in the spatial worldsheet coordinate.

## 6. Relation to the particle limit

If the deformation and background are independent of the string’s spatial coordinate, and the extrinsic string contributions reduce appropriately, the worldsheet Jacobi PDE collapses to the ordinary geodesic Jacobi ODE. In this sense,
\[
\text{geodesic deviation}
\subset
\text{extremal-surface deviation}.
\]

One may also regard a string history as a trajectory in the infinite-dimensional space of loops. Then generalized conjugacy corresponds to conjugacy in string configuration space: the linearized evolution operator develops a zero mode.

## 7. Main conceptual change

The essential extension is:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Particle} & \text{Nambu--Goto string}\\ \hline
\text{Geodesic curve} & \text{Extremal worldsheet}\\
\text{Transverse vector }\xi^\mu(\tau) & \text{Normal field }\Phi^i(\tau,\sigma)\\
\text{Jacobi ODE} & \text{Normal-bundle Jacobi PDE}\\
\text{Riemann tidal term} & \text{Riemann + extrinsic-curvature terms}\\
\text{Conjugate points} & \text{Conjugate slices/configurations or focal sets}
\end{array}
\]

So the theory survives essentially intact, but becomes a field theory on the worldsheet: conjugacy and focusing are controlled by the kernel of the second-variation operator for the Nambu–Goto area functional.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the mathematical framework for varying surfaces spanned by closed strings, including the geodesic surface equation, its Jacobi equation, and the associated index form.
counterfactuals.output:
Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold and let a closed string sweep out a surface
\[
X:\Sigma=S^1\times [0,T]\longrightarrow M,
\qquad X(\sigma+2\pi,\tau)=X(\sigma,\tau).
\]
Write \(X_\sigma=dX(\partial_\sigma)\) and \(X_\tau=dX(\partial_\tau)\).

## 1. Surface functional and geodesic-surface equation

A convenient starting point is the Dirichlet energy
\[
E[X]=\frac12\int_\Sigma
\left(|X_\sigma|^2+|X_\tau|^2\right)\,d\sigma\,d\tau .
\]
Its Euler–Lagrange equation is the harmonic-map, or geodesic-surface, equation
\[
\tau(X):=\nabla_\sigma X_\sigma+\nabla_\tau X_\tau=0,
\]
or in local coordinates,
\[
\partial_\sigma^2X^\mu+\partial_\tau^2X^\mu
+\Gamma^\mu_{\nu\rho}(X)
\left(
\partial_\sigma X^\nu\partial_\sigma X^\rho+
\partial_\tau X^\nu\partial_\tau X^\rho
\right)=0.
\]

If conformal constraints
\[
\langle X_\sigma,X_\tau\rangle=0,
\qquad
|X_\sigma|=|X_\tau|
\]
are imposed, the energy equals the area, and the equation is equivalent to vanishing mean curvature,
\[
H=0.
\]
Thus the worldsheet is a minimal surface. In invariant form for the induced metric \(h=X^*g\),
\[
\operatorname{tr}_{h}\nabla dX=0.
\]

For a Lorentzian string worldsheet, the corresponding equation has the wave-map sign,
\[
\nabla_\tau X_\tau-\nabla_\sigma X_\sigma=0.
\]

## 2. Variations and the Jacobi equation

Consider a variation \(X_s\) through such surfaces and define the variation field
\[
V=\left.\frac{\partial X_s}{\partial s}\right|_{s=0}.
\]
Linearizing the geodesic-surface equation gives the Jacobi equation
\[
J_XV=0,
\]
where, with a common curvature convention,
\[
J_XV=
\nabla_\sigma\nabla_\sigma V+
\nabla_\tau\nabla_\tau V+
R(V,X_\sigma)X_\sigma+
R(V,X_\tau)X_\tau.
\]
Equivalently, for an orthonormal frame \(\{e_a\}\) on \(\Sigma\),
\[
J_XV=
\operatorname{tr}_\Sigma
\left(\nabla^2V+R(V,dX(\,\cdot\,))dX(\,\cdot\,)\right).
\]
The field is periodic in the string coordinate:
\[
V(\sigma+2\pi,\tau)=V(\sigma,\tau),
\]
and it usually vanishes at \(\tau=0,T\) when the initial and final strings are fixed.

For a minimal immersion, only the normal component \(V^\perp\) describes a genuine geometric deformation. The normal Jacobi operator is
\[
J^\perp V
=
\Delta^\perp V+
\sum_{a=1}^{2}
\bigl(R(V,e_a)e_a\bigr)^\perp
+
\mathcal A V,
\]
where
\[
\langle \mathcal A V,W\rangle
=
\sum_{a,b=1}^{2}
\langle A(e_a,e_b),V\rangle
\langle A(e_a,e_b),W\rangle,
\]
\(A\) is the second fundamental form, and \(\Delta^\perp\) is the normal-bundle Laplacian. A Jacobi field satisfies \(J^\perp V=0\).

## 3. Index form

The second variation defines the index form. For fields \(V,W\) satisfying the relevant boundary and periodicity conditions, the harmonic-map index form is
\[
I(V,W)=
\int_\Sigma
\left[
\langle\nabla_\sigma V,\nabla_\sigma W\rangle
+\langle\nabla_\tau V,\nabla_\tau W\rangle
-\langle R(V,X_\sigma)X_\sigma,W\rangle
-\langle R(V,X_\tau)X_\tau,W\rangle
\right]d\sigma\,d\tau .
\]
After integration by parts,
\[
I(V,W)=-\int_\Sigma \langle J_XV,W\rangle\,d\sigma\,d\tau,
\]
up to boundary terms, which vanish for periodic/fixed-boundary variations.

For normal variations of a minimal surface,
\[
I^\perp(V,W)=
\int_\Sigma
\left[
\langle\nabla^\perp V,\nabla^\perp W\rangle
-\sum_a\langle R(V,e_a)e_a,W\rangle
-\langle\mathcal A V,W\rangle
\right]d\mu_h .
\]
In particular,
\[
I^\perp(V,V)=
\int_\Sigma
\left(
|\nabla^\perp V|^2
-\sum_a\langle R(V,e_a)e_a,V\rangle
-\sum_{a,b}|\langle A(e_a,e_b),V\rangle|^2
\right)d\mu_h .
\]

The surface is stable when \(I^\perp(V,V)\ge 0\) for all admissible normal variations. Negative directions give its Morse index, while zero directions are Jacobi fields and represent infinitesimal families of nearby geodesic/minimal worldsheets.
